verses.commentary: Woe (hoy) to the city of blood. Nineveh characterized by violence. Full of lies (deception in diplomacy), full of plunder (theft from conquered peoples), never without victims (perpetual predation). The city's identity is bloodshed.
Sound effects of battle. Crack of whips, clatter of wheels, galloping horses, jolting chariots. The poetry creates an audio experience of warfare. Readers hear the approaching doom.

Charging cavalry, flashing swords, glittering spears. Then the aftermath: many casualties, piles of dead, bodies without number, people stumbling over corpses. The visual follows the auditory. War's reality unvarnished.

The cause: wanton lust of a prostitute. Alluring, mistress of sorceries. Nations enslaved by prostitution, peoples by witchcraft. Nineveh's seductive power: economic, political, religious deception. The city lured nations into submission.

'I am against you' repeated from 2:13. Skirts lifted over face, nakedness shown to nations, shame revealed to kingdoms. The seductress stripped and shamed. Public humiliation reverses public seduction.
Pelted with filth, treated with contempt, made a spectacle. Garbage thrown at the disgraced prostitute. Public ridicule. The powerful city becomes an object of scorn. Honor reversed to shame.

All who see flee. Nineveh in ruins, who will mourn? Where can anyone find comfort for you? Rhetorical questions emphasizing abandonment. No mourners, no comforters. Complete isolation. Those who suffered under Assyria will not grieve its fall.
Are you better than Thebes (No Amon)? Egyptian city on the Nile, protected by water. The river was her defense, waters her wall. Nineveh knows Thebes' fate because Assyria destroyed it in 663 BC.
Cush and Egypt were Thebes' boundless strength. Put and Libya were allies. Massive resources, powerful allies. Yet none of it saved Thebes. Nineveh should learn from what Nineveh inflicted.

Yet Thebes went into exile. Infants dashed at street corners. Nobles divided by lot. Great men chained. Assyria's own brutality now described as precedent for Assyria's fate. History teaches, but tyrants don't learn.
You too will become drunk (staggering under judgment), hide, seek refuge from enemies. The hunter hides. The conqueror seeks shelter. Role reversal prophesied and fulfilled.

Fortresses like fig trees with first ripe fruit. Shake them and figs fall into the eater's mouth. Defenses that seem strong collapse easily. The image combines harvest joy with military conquest. Nineveh's walls are ripe for taking.
Troops are weaklings. Gates of the land wide open. Fire has consumed gate bars. The masculine military power feminized in mocking language. Defenses already breached. The city lies exposed.

Ironic commands again. Draw siege water, strengthen defenses, work clay, tread mortar, repair brickwork! Make preparations, but they will accomplish nothing. Futility of human effort against divine decree.

Fire will consume, sword will cut down. Devoured like locust swarms. Multiply like grasshoppers, multiply like locusts! Ironic: multiply, but it won't help. Numbers mean nothing against divine judgment.
Merchants multiplied more than stars in the sky. Nineveh was a commercial hub. But like locusts, they strip the land and fly away. Merchants flee with wealth. Commerce provides no loyalty.

Guards like locusts, officials like locust swarms. They settle on walls in cold weather, but when sun rises, they fly away. Disappear, no one knows where. Officials desert. Bureaucracy evaporates. The state apparatus vanishes.

King of Assyria, your shepherds slumber. Nobles lie down. People scattered on mountains with no one to gather. Leadership asleep or dead. The flock dispersed. No recovery possible. The metaphor of shepherd failure condemns royal negligence.

Nothing can heal you. The wound is fatal. All who hear the news clap their hands. Who has not felt your endless cruelty? Applause at Nineveh's fall. Universal rejoicing. The book ends with the world celebrating Assyria's destruction. Evil's end brings relief to all who suffered.
